lead: Line coding is the rule that turns a PCM bit stream into voltage or current levels on a baseband link. It exists because the receiver must recover both bits and timing from a waveform that may pass through cables, transformers and AC-coupled circuits. NRZ, RZ and Manchester are the three basic schemes; they trade DC content, clock recovery and spectral width. You meet them in PCM links, TDM backplanes and legacy Ethernet.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.4 PCM bit stream and Chapter 4.7 TDM; Unit 5 pulse shaping and Nyquist bandwidth.

blocks.text: Line code maps each bit, or group of bits, to a level for one bit duration Tb. Rb = 1/Tb is the bit rate in bit/s. V is a fixed peak level in volts.
Three families. Unipolar uses 0 and +V. Polar uses +V and −V. Bipolar (AMI) uses +V, 0 and −V, and alternates the sign for successive 1s.

NRZ means no return to zero: the level lasts the full Tb. Unipolar NRZ sends 1 = +V, 0 = 0. Polar NRZ-L sends 1 = +V, 0 = −V. NRZ-I changes level at the start of a 1 and keeps level for a 0; data sits in transitions, not absolute level.
RZ returns to zero in the second half of every bit. Polar RZ sends 1 = +V then 0, 0 = −V then 0. Unipolar RZ sends 1 = +V then 0, 0 = 0 then 0.

Manchester splits each bit into two halves with opposite levels. With 1 = low-to-high and 0 = high-to-low, every bit has a centre transition. Some syllabi call it biphase or split-phase. Differential Manchester always has the centre transition; the start-of-bit transition, present or absent, carries the data. It is also called CDP.
For 10110, polar NRZ is +V, −V, +V, +V, −V; RZ adds a zero in each second half; Manchester is low-high, high-low, low-high, low-high, high-low.

Power spectral density (PSD) shows how signal power spreads over frequency. For equally likely polar NRZ with rectangular pulses, pNRZ(f) = V2 Tb sinc2(f Tb), where pNRZ(f) is the PSD in W/Hz, V is the peak level in volts, Tb is the bit duration in seconds, f is frequency in Hz, and sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx). The first null is at f = 1/Tb = Rb. The main lobe runs from 0 to Rb.
Unipolar NRZ has a similar sinc² shape but also a discrete component at DC, because its mean level is not zero. Polar NRZ has zero mean only when 1 and 0 are equally likely and levels are symmetric.

RZ uses a pulse of width T<sub>b</sub>/2, so its first null is at 2Rb. Manchester uses two half-bit levels; its PSD contains a half-bit sinc² factor multiplied by sin²(πfT<sub>b</sub>/2), which forces zero at DC for equal bits. Its first null is at 2Rb, and the symbol rate is 2Rb. Differential Manchester has the same bandwidth.

Bandwidth efficiency: NRZ gives the narrowest main lobe for a given Rb. RZ and Manchester need about twice the bandwidth. A full PSD derivation from the autocorrelation is advanced; only a few universities teach it.

The receiver needs a clock at Rb to sample each bit at its centre. A clock-recovery circuit, often a phase-locked loop, locks to transitions in the received waveform. Long runs of 1s or 0s in NRZ have no transitions, so the clock can drift and bits slip.

RZ returns to zero every bit, so it supplies a transition. Manchester supplies a guaranteed centre transition every bit, so it is self-synchronising. Differential Manchester also has a centre transition every bit. Manchester is used where the clock must be recovered through AC coupling, because every bit has a centre transition. Where the pair may be swapped (polarity inversion), differential Manchester is the safer choice: its data lives in the start-of-bit transition, so inverted wires give the same bits, while plain Manchester would read them inverted.

The cost is bandwidth and symbol rate. Manchester needs two half-bit levels per bit, so it is less bandwidth-efficient than NRZ. NRZ has the narrowest main lobe but needs scrambling or framing to break long runs. RZ and Manchester both cost about twice the bandwidth; RZ buys one transition per bit, Manchester buys a guaranteed centre transition and zero DC. See Unit 5 for pulse shaping and intersymbol interference.

examples.question: A binary sequence 1 0 1 1 0 is sent at 1 kbit/s. Find the bit duration and the first spectral null of polar NRZ, RZ and Manchester. State which code has no DC and self-clocking. Use the convention 1 = low-to-high, 0 = high-to-low for Manchester.
steps: Polar NRZ first null: f1 = 1/Tb = 1/0.001 = 1000 Hz = 1 kHz.
RZ first null: f2 = 2/Tb = 2/0.001 = 2000 Hz = 2 kHz.
Manchester uses two half-bit levels per bit, so symbol rate = 2Rb = 2000 symbol/s; first null f3 = 2/Tb = 2000 Hz = 2 kHz.

Manchester has equal positive and negative halves for any data pattern, so zero DC; it has a centre transition every bit, so it is self-clocking. Polar RZ is also DC-free for equally likely bits and gives one transition per bit; Manchester is singled out because it is DC-free for any data pattern and its centre transition is guaranteed whatever the bits.
examples.answer: The bit duration is 0.001 s (1 ms); the first nulls are 1000 Hz (1 kHz) for polar NRZ and 2000 Hz (2 kHz) for RZ and Manchester; Manchester is the code asked for: it is DC-free for any data pattern and self-clocking. Polar RZ is also DC-free for equally likely bits and gives one transition per bit.
examples.check:
Rb = 1000
Tb = 1 / Rb
f_nrz = 1 / Tb
f_rz = 2 / Tb
f_man = 2 / Tb
print(Tb)
print(f_nrz)
print(f_rz)
print(f_man)

traps: For Manchester the symbol rate is 2Rb because each bit has two half-bit levels; the first null is 2Rb, not Rb.
Long runs of 1s or 0s in NRZ cause clock loss; RZ and Manchester restore transitions at a bandwidth cost.
Do not call unipolar NRZ DC-free: for equally likely bits its mean is V/2, so it has a DC component.
NRZ-I is not NRZ-L: NRZ-I stores data in transitions, NRZ-L in absolute level. Differential Manchester is not plain Manchester: data is in the start transition, not the centre-transition direction.

quiz.q: Define unipolar, polar and bipolar line codes.
quiz.a: Unipolar uses 0 and +V. Polar uses +V and −V. Bipolar uses +V, 0 and −V, with alternating sign for successive 1s.

quiz.q: Why is Manchester described as self-clocking?
quiz.a: Every bit has a guaranteed centre transition, so the receiver can extract a clock at the bit rate even during long runs of the same bit.

quiz.q: A polar NRZ link sends 10 kbit/s. Find the bit duration and the first spectral null.
quiz.a: Rb = 10000 bit/s; Tb = 1/Rb = 0.0001 s = 0.1 ms; first null = 1/Tb = 10 kHz.

quiz.q: Bits 1011 are sent at 2 kbit/s in Manchester. Find the bit duration and the first null.
quiz.a: Rb = 2000 bit/s; Tb = 1/2000 = 0.0005 s = 0.5 ms; Manchester first null = 2Rb = 4 kHz.

quiz.q: Why can a long run of 1s cause clock loss in NRZ, and how does RZ help?
quiz.a: A long run of 1s has no level transitions, so a clock-recovery loop has nothing to lock to and drifts. RZ returns to zero in every bit, creating a transition in each bit period, so the clock stays aligned.

quiz.q: In terms of Rb, where is the first spectral null of RZ?
quiz.a: At 2Rb, because the RZ pulse width is Tb/2.

quiz.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of differential Manchester compared with NRZ.
quiz.a: Advantage: it is self-clocking and DC-free, and data is read from start transitions so polarity inversion does not matter. Disadvantage: it needs about twice the bandwidth of NRZ and has a higher symbol rate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Manchester coding appears in legacy 10 Mbit/s Ethernet and some industrial and isolation links because its DC-free, self-clocking waveform passes through transformers. Modern high-speed links use multilevel codes, scramblers and DSP rather than plain NRZ or Manchester. Search next for line-code spectral density, 8b/10b, 64b/66b and MLT-3. These ideas connect to SerDes and backplane design in industry.
